clue.text: Batting with twelve, one requiring treatment?

parts.note: a batter at the crease in cricket is said to be in
a jury is made up of twelve people

explanation.surface: A cricketer going in to bat with eleven teammates, one of them hurt and needing a medic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batting with twelve' reads as cricket, but it is IN (at the crease) beside JURY (a panel of twelve).
explanation.definitionFit: A wound or hurt is something a doctor would treat, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Warm for a while on an island, followed by extremes of temperature

parts.note: on in the sense of happening or present gives in
Cuba is an island in the Caribbean

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, so take the ends of temperature

explanation.surface: Sunbathing on a Caribbean island where the temperature swings wildly.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep eggs or cultures warm for a period so they develop is to brood them over time.

clue.text: Flier, beast that's grey and black

parts.note: Jumbo is a stock name for an elephant, a grey beast
jet is a deep black colour, as in jet-black

explanation.surface: A bird described by its grey and black plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: A large passenger airliner is something that flies, so it is a flier.

clue.text: Hand action in the throne room?

definitions.meaning: in poker a hand of ace, king, queen, jack and ten of one suit
the throne is slang for the toilet, so a ... room's toilet being ... is a pun on the phrase

explanation.surface: Something done by hand in a palace's throne room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throne room' is a jokey name for a lavatory; the action there is a flush, and in a palace a royal one.
explanation.definitionFit: The top poker holding of ace to ten in one suit is a hand of cards.

clue.text: Train service, where routes abroad on a railway starting out

indicators.note: abroad in its old sense of scattered widely, so the letters of routes are spread about
starting out points to the opening letter of the word railway

explanation.surface: A train service whose routes go abroad on a railway that is just getting going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' is the anagram signal, in its old sense of scattered widely; 'starting out' takes only the first letter of 'railway'.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-Channel rail link between London and the Continent is a passenger train operator.

clue.text: Memorable number?

definitions.meaning: something memorable can never be forgotten
a number is a song; this is the classic Nat King Cole song of that title

explanation.definitionFit: Something memorable sticks in the mind permanently, and the word also names a famous popular song.

clue.text: Beethoven's Fifth creators, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be arranged in another way
the fifth letter of the word Beethoven is wanted here

explanation.surface: Those who created Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifth letter of BEETHOVEN is H; mixed with CREATORS 'possibly' gives the answer, and the whole clue describes those who perform (create the sound of) the symphony.
explanation.definitionFit: A symphony is brought to life in performance by the full band of musicians who play it.

clue.text: Article I've wrongly pocketed — to do this?

definitions.text: Article I've wrongly pocketed — to do this?

indicators.note: pocketed means held inside, so one piece sits within the article

parts.note: the is the definite article

indicators.note: wrongly tells us the letters of I've are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A confession of having wrongly pocketed something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' signals the anagram and 'pocketed' the container; read as a whole, the clue describes the very act of stealing an article.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrongly pocketing an article is stealing, which is what the verb means.

clue.text: Dashing from shark at sea, one getting caught

indicators.note: getting caught means being held inside the other letters
at sea means confused or disordered, so the letters of shark are jumbled

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Swimmers dashing away from a shark at sea, one of them caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' makes RAKSH from SHARK, and the I goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dashing man is stylishly jaunty and a little roguish.

clue.text: Firm mattresses first yielding, each starting out as soft

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: each starting out takes the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Firm mattresses, once they first give, start out feeling soft.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfortable, cosy furniture or bedding is soft and pleasant to sit or lie on.

clue.text: As a computer operator, touch went cold with gentle stroke

parts.note: went in the sense of departed gives left
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
a lick is a light stroke, as of paint

explanation.surface: Someone touching another person, who goes cold under a gentle caress.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing the primary mouse button is how a computer user touches an item on screen.

clue.text: Red-hot stuff on the Telegraph, politically? That's the Daily Mail to Guardian readers!

definitions.text: That's the Daily Mail to Guardian readers!

parts.note: lava is molten red-hot rock from a volcano
the Daily Telegraph is a British newspaper that backs the Conservatives, the Tories

explanation.surface: A media jibe: one right-wing paper sits beside another, and left-leaning readers scorn the Daily Mail.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Telegraph and the Daily Mail are right-leaning British newspapers; the Guardian is a left-leaning one whose readers might think the Mail fit only for the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A scornful reader might say a disliked newspaper is fit only for wiping in the toilet.

clue.text: South African carries fine volume back — for one who'd appreciate it?

indicators.note: carries means holds within, so the other pieces go inside

parts.note: a Boer is a South African of Dutch descent
OK means fine or all right

indicators.note: back means the abbreviation for volume is read the other way

explanation.surface: A South African carrying a fine book back to someone who'd value it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carries' is the container and 'back' the reversal; the 'it' that the definition's reader appreciates is the volume itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who adores reading would value a fine volume, so the volume is the 'it' they appreciate.

clue.text: Incomplete permission to enter for Felipe, the king

parts.note: Felipe is a Spanish name, and the Spanish for 'the' is el

indicators.note: incomplete means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a visa is official permission to enter a country

explanation.surface: A Spaniard named Felipe denied full entry, with the king mentioned.
explanation.definitionFit: The rock and roll singer from Memphis was nicknamed the King.

clue.text: As you see, normal scores

definitions.meaning: normal eyesight is described by the score of twenty over twenty on an eye chart
a score is twenty, so two scores are twenty and twenty

explanation.surface: As you can see, these results are ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect ordinary eyesight is measured on the Snellen chart, and a pair of scores is forty.

clue.text: Sweet packet is empty, finally screwed up

indicators.note: screwed up means crumpled or messed up, so these letters are rearranged
finally points to the last letter of the word empty

explanation.surface: A sweet wrapper, now empty, finally crumpled and tossed.
explanation.walkthrough: TIPSY CAKE is a British dessert of sponge soaked in sherry or wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A boozy sponge pudding is a dessert, which British speakers call a sweet.

clue.text: Event in trouble for it?

definitions.meaning: an athletics field event in which competitors leap a bar
a British idiom for being about to be punished

explanation.surface: An occasion where someone is going to get into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the high jump' is British slang for about to be punished.
explanation.definitionFit: The bar-clearing leap is one of the contests at an athletics meeting.

clue.text: Celeb's cool craft that's out of this world

definitions.text: craft that's out of this world

parts.note: a celeb is a star, so celeb's gives star's
hip means cool or fashionable

explanation.surface: A celebrity's trendy, amazing vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel built to travel in space beyond Earth is a craft out of this world in the literal sense.

clue.text: Medium habit is coming in double

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so these pieces go inside the double

parts.note: spit means a double or exact likeness, as in the spitting image
a ritual is a fixed habit or routine

explanation.surface: A medium-sized habit, a monk's garment, arriving in a double size.
explanation.definitionFit: A medium is a person who claims to pass messages from the dead, a séance practitioner.

clue.text: Mammoth on back of car?

definitions.meaning: mammoth means huge, as in a huge crop or harvest
the protective bar fitted on the rear of a motor

explanation.surface: A woolly mammoth seen riding on the back of a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge harvest or crowd is called a bumper one, and the guard bar sits at a car's rear.

clue.text: A piece of cake for eating outdoors

definitions.meaning: an idiom for something very easy
a meal eaten in the open air

explanation.surface: A slice of cake packed for eating outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something no trouble at all is a doddle, and an open-air meal on a rug has the same name.

clue.text: The Mitfords' fascist agreement

explanation.walkthrough: The Mitfords were six famous British aristocratic sisters of the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: One Mitford sister was a notorious Nazi sympathiser, and the same word means concord or oneness.

clue.text: Dealer going about business with literary intentions, initially?

definitions.text: Dealer going about business with literary intentions, initially?

indicators.note: going about means surrounding, so the dealer wraps round the other letters

parts.note: a pusher is a drug dealer

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of each of the words business, literary and intentions

explanation.surface: A trader who conducts business with literary aims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' picks the first letters and 'going about' wraps the dealer round them; 'with' is just a link. Read whole, the clue describes a book trader.
explanation.definitionFit: A company that trades in books does business with literary aims.

clue.text: Conclude there's sign of fear, every second

indicators.note: every second means taking the second, fourth and later letters in turn

explanation.surface: Deducing that someone is afraid from every passing sign.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a conclusion from evidence is to deduce it.

clue.text: Fruit that may go off?

definitions.meaning: a tropical fruit with a spiky skin
slang for a hand grenade, which explodes

explanation.surface: A fruit that might go rotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' suggests rotting fruit, but here it means explode: a pineapple is slang for a hand grenade.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiky tropical fruit is also a nickname for a grenade, which explodes.

clue.text: See 3
Little time in garden for astronautical science

indicators.note: in tells us one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a rockery is a rock garden
T is the short form of time

explanation.surface: Spending a little time in the garden studying space science.
explanation.definitionFit: The study and building of rockets is the science behind space flight.

clue.text: Bring a graceless halt to mountaineering expedition?

definitions.meaning: to make someone stumble and stop clumsily
read literally, a journey up a mountain

explanation.surface: Ending a climbing expedition clumsily.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone stumble or catch them out stops them awkwardly, and a climb is a journey upward.
